content: An estimated one-third of the global population is infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Each year, approximately 9 million individuals develop active tuberculosis (TB) disease caused by this bacterium. While TB predominantly affects resource-limited countries, it also occurs in the United States. Between 1985 and 1992, the United States experienced an unprecedented resurgence of TB, accompanied by an increase in multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). MDR-TB is defined as TB that is resistant to the two most effective first-line drugs, isoniazid and rifampin. Furthermore, strains of M. tuberculosis that are virtually untreatable are emerging globally. Extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) is a subset of MDR-TB that is also resistant to the most effective second-line drugs, including fluoroquinolones and at least one of three injectable second-line drugs (amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin). XDR-TB has been identified in all regions of the world, including the United States. In the United States, the average cost of hospitalization for a single XDR-TB patient is estimated at $483,000, which is approximately double the cost for MDR-TB patients. Due to the limited effectiveness of available antibiotics against XDR-TB, mortality rates among XDR-TB patients are comparable to those seen in the pre-antibiotic era. In January 1992, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) convened a Federal TB Task Force to develop an action plan aimed at improving the prevention and control of drug-resistant TB in the United States. In November 2006, the CDC reconvened the Task Force to update the action plan to address MDR-TB and XDR-TB. Task Force members were divided into nine response areas to identify pressing problems, barriers to improvement, and specific action steps to enhance prevention and control of XDR-TB. Although the primary focus of the 2006 Task Force was to address MDR-TB and XDR-TB domestically, members recognized the importance of collaborating with the international community to strengthen global TB control efforts. TB remains a significant public health issue in lowand middle-income countries, many of which could benefit from assistance provided by the United States. Additionally, the global TB epidemic directly impacts the United States, as the majority of TB cases and 80% of MDR-TB cases reported in the U.S. occur among foreign-born individuals. Unless the root causes of MDR-TB and XDR-TB are addressed both domestically and internationally, the United States is likely to face an increasing number of cases that will be challenging, if not impossible, to treat or prevent. The recommendations outlined in the updated action plan include specific steps and new activities that require additional funding and a renewed commitment from government and non-government organizations involved in TB control efforts. TB is one of the most common infectious diseases and a leading cause of death worldwide. It is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is primarily transmitted through airborne droplets. While TB can affect any part of the body, it most commonly involves the lungs. Individuals with pulmonary TB typically have a cough that produces airborne droplet nuclei containing the bacteria, which can remain suspended in the air for hours. Vulnerable individuals exposed to these droplets may become infected. Most infected individuals remain asymptomatic and non-contagious, a condition known as latent TB infection (LTBI). LTBI can be treated with a single drug, isoniazid, for nine months to prevent progression to active disease. Without treatment, individuals with LTBI have a 5-10% lifetime risk of developing active TB, though this risk increases significantly in the presence of immunosuppression, such as HIV infection or immunosuppressive medications. Pulmonary TB can be cured with a six-month course of antibiotics, including isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol during the initial two months. In the United States, TB diagnosis and treatment are accessible and effective. However, many developing countries lack the resources to diagnose and treat TB effectively. Globally, approximately 2 billion people (one-third of the world's population) are estimated to have LTBI. Nearly 9 million individuals develop active TB disease annually, resulting in close to 2 million TB-related deaths each year. In the United States, approximately 13,000 new TB cases are reported annually, with 650 deaths attributed to TB each year. TB is the leading cause of mortality among individuals infected with HIV. During the 1985-1992 TB resurgence in the United States, a significant number of patients failed to respond to treatment and ultimately died. These cases were identified as MDR-TB, defined as TB resistant to both isoniazid and rifampin. While MDR-TB can often be treated with second-line drugs (amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin), these drugs are associated with more side effects, are more expensive, and are less effective than first-line drugs. Treatment regimens for MDR-TB typically last 18-24 months, and the cure rate is only 50-60%, compared to 95-97% for drug-susceptible TB. In response to MDR-TB outbreaks, the Federal TB Task Force published an action plan in 1992, outlining specific steps for state and local health departments and federal agencies. These steps were grouped into nine categories, including surveillance, laboratory diagnosis, patient management, screening and preventive therapy, infection control, outbreak control, program evaluation, information dissemination/training and education, and research. Emergency federal funding was allocated to implement parts of the plan, leading to significant improvements in diagnostic capacity, surveillance systems, infection control practices, and treatment protocols. Since 1993, the incidence of TB and the total number of TB cases in the United States have decreased, although the rate of decline has slowed since 2000. Globally, the number of TB cases has continued to rise, but the incidence rate has decreased since 2003. However, highly drug-resistant forms of TB, including XDR-TB, have emerged worldwide. In 2006, the CDC, World Health Organization (WHO), and the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease (IUATLD) reported that 20% of M. tuberculosis isolates were MDR, and 2% were resistant to multiple second-line drugs. XDR-TB was identified in every region of the world, including the United States, where 4% of MDR-TB isolates were resistant to multiple second-line drugs. The emergence of XDR-TB raises concerns about potential epidemics of virtually untreatable TB, which could result in excessive mortality and substantial financial and infrastructure burdens for public health and TB control programs. XDR-TB is significantly more expensive to treat, with hospitalization costs in the United States averaging $483,000 per case. A major XDR-TB outbreak in the United States would strain public health resources, deplete state and local TB budgets, and hinder progress toward TB elimination. Treatment failures and subsequent deaths are more common among XDR-TB patients, and the drugs available for treatment are associated with serious adverse effects. In countries with high HIV prevalence and limited healthcare resources, substantial numbers of XDR-TB cases are likely present. However, many drug-resistant cases go undetected due to limited access to culture and susceptibility testing. The emergence of XDR-TB highlights the need for urgent action to strengthen TB control efforts, enhance diagnostic and treatment capacity, and address the ethical and legal challenges associated with managing drug-resistant TB.
